q: How many Grand Crus does Alsace have, and what is legally unusual about them?
accept: 51 and each one is its own appellation
fifty one grand crus each a separate aoc with its own rules
each grand cru is legally its own aoc with its own decree
ans: Fifty-one, and each is a separate AOC in its own right with its own decree setting permitted varieties, yields and minimum ripeness — Kaefferkopf, added in 2007, was the last admitted
exp: Because each cru is written individually, the rules differ: Zotzenberg permits Sylvaner, Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf permit blends, and the usual four-noble-grape restriction is not universal. Note too that the term is optional — Trimbach's Clos Ste Hune sits in Rosacker and has historically declined to say so, which is a reminder that a classification only tells you what the producer chose to claim.

q: Give South Africa's Wine of Origin hierarchy from the largest unit to the smallest.
accept: geographical unit then region then district then ward
geographical unit region district ward plus estate and single vineyard
from geographical unit down to ward
ans: Geographical Unit (Western Cape) → Region (Coastal Region) → District (Stellenbosch) → Ward (Simonsberg-Stellenbosch); Estate Wine and registered Single Vineyard sit alongside as separate claims rather than as tiers
exp: WO certifies claims, it does not dictate style: origin must be 100 per cent, variety and vintage 85 per cent for export, and there are no rules on grape, yield or method — much closer to an Australian GI than to an AOP. A registered Single Vineyard is capped at six hectares and a single variety. The certification seal on the capsule is what carries the guarantee.

q: How many Grand Cru and Premier Cru villages does Champagne have, and what became of the échelle des crus?
accept: 17 grand cru and 42 premier cru villages and the price scale is gone
seventeen grand crus forty two premier crus the echelle is defunct
17 grand crus 42 premier crus rated on a percentage scale no longer used
the villages remain classified but the pricing ladder was abolished
ans: Seventeen Grand Cru and forty-two Premier Cru villages; the échelle was a percentage price scale rating each village up to 100 per cent, and it was abandoned as a pricing mechanism around 2010, leaving the cru names as heritage classifications only
exp: Champagne classifies whole communes, not plots, so grand cru status covers every hectare in the village including its indifferent land — the opposite of Burgundy's plot-by-plot ranking. And since grape prices are now negotiated between grower and house, the rating is reputational rather than economic. A wine may say Grand Cru only if all its fruit comes from those villages.

q: Since the 2013 vintage, Tokaji Aszú must contain a minimum residual sugar of:
exp: The 2013 reform abolished the 3 and 4 puttonyos categories outright and set the Aszú floor at 120 g/l — what used to be 5 puttonyos. Producers may still print 5 puttonyos (from 120 g/l) or 6 puttonyos (from 150 g/l) if they wish, but Aszú alone now guarantees the old 5-puttonyos level. Eszencia, made from free-run juice of aszú berries, needs at least 450 g/l and barely ferments past a couple of degrees of alcohol.

q: Why does umami-rich food harden many red wines?
ans: Umami amplifies perceived tannin and bitterness while flattening fruit
exp: Salt is the antidote — hence cheese's rescue act, and bubbles' success with dashi and mushroom.

q: Capsaicin heat interacts with alcohol by:
ans: Ethanol amplifies the burn (both trigger TRPV1) — reach for low-alcohol, off-dry, cold
exp: Kabinett Riesling and Moscato d'Asti are the fire brigade.

q: Match the impossible ingredient to its rescue.
exp: Cynarin makes the next sip taste falsely sweet; Fino shrugs.

q: Classic law: the wine must be sweeter than the dish. Violate it and:
ans: The wine reads thin, sour and bitter against the sugar
exp: Why demi-sec dies against chocolate cake but Banyuls thrives.

q: Blue cheese and Sauternes work through which mechanism?
ans: Salt-fat pungency against sweetness and acid — amplified contrast, mutual flattery
exp: Roquefort-Sauternes and Stilton-Port are the two canonical marriages.

q: Best structural logic for raw oysters:
accept: high acid saline no oak low alcohol
ans: High acid, saline echo, no oak, modest alcohol: Muscadet sur lie, Chablis, Fino, brut nature fizz
exp: Metallic clash risk comes from tannin and oak, not white wine per se.

q: Game birds with earthy notes (grouse, squab) call classically for:
ans: Mature Pinot Noir/Burgundy (or Nebbiolo) — forest-floor echoing forest flavor
exp: 'Echo' pairings match tertiary notes to gamey depth.

q: Sushi's pairing hazards are soy (salt/umami) and wasabi (heat). The pro answers:
ans: Sake (umami-native, no tannin), Champagne, dry aromatic whites
exp: Sake never fights soy — the family resemblance wins.

q: High-fat fish (salmon, toro) can carry which red category?
accept: light low tannin chilled reds pinot gamay
ans: Light, low-tannin, chilled reds — Pinot, Gamay, Frappato, Trousseau
exp: Fat buffers tannin; the fishy-metallic aftertaste tracks the wine's iron, not iodine — high-iron, tannic reds are the clash, not reds as a class.

q: Fermented and funky dishes (kimchi, aged cheese rinds, natto) find their best glass in:
accept: funk echoes funk sherry orange sake gueuze
oxidative or skin contact or wild ferments
ans: Fellow ferments: Sherry, orange wine, sake, gueuze — funk harmonizing funk
exp: The 'ferment-to-ferment' principle is modern somm doctrine.

q: Why does salt in the dish flatter tannic wine?
accept: salt suppresses bitterness softens tannin perception
ans: Salt suppresses bitterness perception and softens astringency — steakhouse chemistry in one line
exp: Also why Parmesan rescues austere young Sangiovese.

q: Charred bitter greens — radicchio, grilled chicory, blackened kale — beside a young tannic red do what?
opts: Bitterness compounds and the finish hardens
The char's smoke rounds off the wine's tannin
Bitterness in the food cancels the astringency
The wine's fruit lifts and offsets the bitter
exp: Bitterness is the one element that is simply additive: the dish's bitter compounds and the wine's phenolic bitterness sum rather than cancel. Sweet, salt and umami all modulate each other in interesting ways; bitter plus bitter just gets more bitter. The fix is on the plate — fat, salt or a sweet element in the dressing — or a wine whose grip is resolved rather than raw.
